text: Domain Separation is the real mechanism behind last lesson's default: favor one production instance, and handle multi-tenancy needs within it. It logically walls off data and configuration for genuinely distinct organizational units, all inside a single shared instance.

Every record in a domain-separated instance carries a hidden sys_domain field that determines which domain it belongs to. Subsidiary A's incidents and catalog items stay invisible to Subsidiary B, and vice versa, while a parent-level top domain can still see across both — all without a second production instance.

This exists for two genuinely structural situations: separate subsidiaries under one parent company that share an instance for licensing and operations efficiency but must never see each other's data, and a Managed Service Provider running multiple distinct clients on the exact same tables and scoped applications, where each client's data must stay completely invisible to the other.

Not every table behaves the same way. Domain-separated data is visible only within its own domain, never a sibling's. Domain-extendable data lets the top domain see and edit records in subordinate domains too — which is how an MSP admin manages shared configuration centrally. Getting that choice wrong is exactly how data leaks between domains meant to be airtight.

The honest cost: once Domain Separation is on, every future script, report, and integration has to be written with domain awareness. The same query can return different results depending on the running user's domain, and a script tested from the top domain — which sees everything — can silently misbehave for a subordinate domain's user. That ongoing cost means Domain Separation should only be adopted when a real data-separation requirement demands it, never as a default just because an org has multiple departments. Chapter 8's governance models lesson covers the far more common alternative.

Domain Separation buys real isolation at a real, permanent cost to every future customization. Next: scoped application architecture at enterprise scale, and how many scoped apps an organization should actually maintain.
